technical_issues.where: Project Plan & Preliminary Progress – Orbit Specifics
technical_issues.issue: A geostationary orbit is at about 35,786 km, not 600 km (600 km is LEO). A GEO satellite also sits over the equator, so it cannot remain fixed above the reef at about 10–24°S.

technical_issues.where: Project Plan & Preliminary Progress – Editing & Finalisation vs Image 1
technical_issues.issue: The text reserves weeks 7 and 8 for editing and finalisation, but the Gantt chart schedules Editing & Finalisation in weeks 9 and 10.
The communications and near-real-time relay requirement is not linked to any orbit, link budget or ground-station design, so the space segment is not related to the mission function.

technical_issues.where: Project Plan & Preliminary Progress – Launch Specifics
technical_issues.issue: Launch vehicle, trajectory and site are listed as tasks but no preliminary launch or orbit analysis is presented to support them.

overall: Clear mission motivation with good referencing, but the stated geostationary 600 km orbit is physically incorrect and undermines the concept. The plan has a schedule inconsistency and no explicit contingencies. Preliminary technical results are absent, and the software and information sources are only implicit.

feedback.summary: You have a clear motivation for monitoring Great Barrier Reef bleaching, with a near-real-time relay and scientist users identified and sourced in footnotes. Your Gantt chart makes the plan look feasible. The main problem is the orbit: a 600 km geostationary orbit is not physically possible, and a geostationary satellite cannot stay over the reef. Correcting this and adding evidence of technical results would move your work forward substantially.
next_steps: Correct the orbit. An altitude of 600 km is low Earth orbit, while geostationary orbit sits at about 35,786 km over the equator, so it cannot hover above the reef at 10–24°S. Choose an orbit suited to reef coverage and justify it with a calculation.
Present preliminary technical results, such as orbit calculations, COE/AOE values and annotated STK screenshots, with a short interpretation of each.
Resolve the schedule clash between your text (weeks 7–8) and your Gantt chart (weeks 9–10). Add a contingency for delays and give full source details for your footnotes.

criteria.C1: Your purpose is clear: monitoring reef bleaching, a near-real-time relay and scientist users are all identified, with sources footnoted. To reach the next level, quantify your goals and requirements (for example resolution, revisit time, coverage and mission lifetime) and show how they serve named users and Australian beneficiaries. Your communications requirement also needs linking to an orbit, link budget or ground station. The current orbit contradicts the mission function, so correcting it is essential.
criteria.C2: Your week-based Gantt chart, with status colours and deadlines, makes the plan look feasible. To reach the next level, add provision for variations and contingencies, and explain why the schedule suits the mission narrative. Fix the editing conflict: your text reserves weeks 7–8, but the chart schedules weeks 9–10. Information sources and software are only implicit, so state them explicitly and justify them within the mission context.
criteria.C3: You have made real progress: background reading, the Asner brief and STK tutorials 1–4 are all noted. However, no technical results are shown yet. Include concrete outputs such as orbit calculations, COE/AOE values or STK screenshots, and interpret what each shows. This evidence would show you are clearly on track for completion and move this criterion beyond the lower end of Adequate.
criteria.C4: Your headings and superscript citations matching footnotes make the report easy to follow. To reach a professional standard, add a caption to the Gantt chart and give full source details in footnotes rather than bare URLs. Replace notes-style bullets such as 'Need to decide' and 'More STK simulations needed' with formal wording, and make your section titles consistent.
